summary: Psalm 16 begins with a plea for preservation and a confession that the speaker's good is found in Yahweh. The poem then rejects loyalty to another god, speaks of the portion Yahweh assigns and the secure lot he gives, and moves into confidence, gladness, and hope that God will show the path of life.
whyItMatters: This chapter is a compact trust psalm within Book I of Psalms, where many David-associated prayers move between danger and confidence. It shows how the Psalter can join refuge, worship, loyalty, bodily safety, and hope beyond deathlike threat without pausing to explain every background circumstance.

context.author: Many writers and collections stand behind Psalms. This psalm's heading says, “A Poem by David,” but Davidic headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers debate their exact force.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that adopted the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period; assigning one date to Psalm 16 from this chapter alone would be more precise than the evidence allows.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, a collection dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence. The poem itself does not name a specific event or location.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, here a trust psalm shaped by plea, confession of loyalty, rejection of rival worship, and confident expectation.

outline.heading: Request for refuge
outline.note: The speaker asks God for preservation and confesses Yahweh as Lord and source of good.

outline.heading: Loyalty and refusal
outline.note: The speaker delights in the saints on earth and refuses the worship practices and names of another god.

outline.heading: Assigned portion
outline.note: The speaker describes the portion and cup assigned by Yahweh, a secure lot, and a pleasant inheritance.

outline.heading: Counsel and stability
outline.note: The speaker blesses Yahweh for counsel and says that keeping Yahweh before him gives stability.

outline.heading: Joy and the path of life
outline.note: The poem ends with gladness, bodily safety, confidence about Sheol and corruption, and the promise of life, presence, joy, and lasting pleasures.

keyVerses.text: A Poem by David. Preserve me, God, for I take refuge in you.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the chapter's heading and frames the prayer as a request for protection grounded in refuge.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh assigned my portion and my cup. You made my lot secure.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the middle of the psalm, where security is described with inheritance and allotment language.

keyVerses.text: For you will not leave my soul in Sheol, neither will you allow your holy one to see corruption.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter's most debated line because it speaks of Sheol and corruption, and later Christian readers especially connect it with resurrection; the chapter itself voices confidence that God will not abandon the speaker.

keyVerses.text: You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the psalm's movement into life, divine presence, joy, and lasting delight.

questions.question: What does the heading “A Poem by David” prove?
questions.answer: It proves that the received psalm has a Davidic heading. Such headings may mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, and readers differ over how much historical information each heading preserves. The chapter itself does not narrate an event from David's life.

questions.question: Why does the speaker ask, “Preserve me”?
questions.answer: The chapter does not name the danger. It only shows the speaker asking God for preservation and explaining that he takes refuge in God. That leaves the pressure real but unspecified.

questions.question: What does “Apart from you I have no good thing” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The line places the speaker's good in relation to Yahweh. It does not list every possible good thing in life; it states the speaker's dependence and loyalty. The following verses develop that loyalty by delighting in the saints and refusing another god.

questions.question: Who are “the saints who are on the earth”?
questions.answer: The psalm describes them as “the excellent ones” and says the speaker's delight is in them. The chapter does not define the group more fully. In this context they appear as people with whom the speaker identifies, in contrast to those who give gifts to another god.

questions.question: What is going on with “drink offerings of blood”?
questions.answer: Verse 4 refers to people whose sorrows multiply because they give gifts to another god, and the speaker refuses their drink offerings and their names. The chapter does not describe the ritual in detail. The point within the psalm is separation from rival worship, not a full explanation of ancient offerings.

questions.question: What do “portion,” “cup,” “lot,” and “inheritance” add to the poem?
questions.answer: These words picture the speaker's assigned share and secure future as gifts from Yahweh. The language suggests allotment and possession, and the speaker thanks Yahweh for making his lot secure. The result is contentment: the lines have fallen in pleasant places.

questions.question: How can the speaker say, “I shall not be moved”?
questions.answer: The reason given is that Yahweh is before the speaker and at his right hand. The verse is a statement of confidence, not a claim that faithful people never experience danger or distress. In the immediate flow, stability comes from God's nearness and counsel.

questions.question: Does verse 10 teach resurrection?
questions.answer: The verse says God will not leave the speaker's soul in Sheol or allow his holy one to see corruption. Readers differ on whether, in its first poetic setting, this means rescue from death, rescue through death, or hope beyond death. Later Christian reception reads this line in relation to Jesus' resurrection, but that is a later use of the psalm and should not erase the chapter's own voice of trust.

questions.question: What is “the path of life” at the end?
questions.answer: Verse 11 says God will show the speaker the path of life and links it with God's presence, fullness of joy, and pleasures at God's right hand. The psalm does not map the path in steps. It ends by placing life and joy with God rather than with another source of security.

glossary.def: A place or relationship of protection. In verse 1 the speaker asks to be preserved because he takes refuge in God.
The people in whom the speaker delights, called “the excellent ones” in verse 3.
An assigned share. In verse 5, the speaker credits Yahweh with assigning his portion and cup and making his lot secure.
The realm or condition associated with the dead in the poem's language. Verse 10 says God will not leave the speaker's soul there.
Decay or ruin associated here with death. Verse 10 says God will not allow his holy one to see it.
